reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Defined by antibodies to aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (most commonly anti-Jo-1) together with a characteristic clinical constellation
The typical features are inflammatory myositis, interstitial lung disease, non-erosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and 'mechanic's hands'
Interstitial lung disease is frequently the dominant and prognosis-determining manifestation and may occur without overt muscle weakness (amyopathic presentations)
Mechanic's hands describes hyperkeratotic, fissured, roughened skin along the radial and palmar aspects of the fingers
Non-anti-Jo-1 antibodies (anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-EJ, anti-OJ) may present with more prominent lung disease and less myositis
Creatine kinase is usually elevated when myositis is active, and myositis-specific antibody panels aid diagnosis
Management centres on systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppression, tailored to the severity of lung and muscle involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Antisynthetase syndrome is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by autoantibodies directed against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzymes, which normally catalyse the attachment of amino acids to their transfer RNA during protein synthesis. In genetically predisposed individuals, an environmental trigger is thought to provoke an immune response against these cytoplasmic enzymes, generating both a humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated attack. The resulting inflammation targets skeletal muscle, the lung interstitium, joints, and skin, producing myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and mechanic's hands.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis and dermatomyositis) without synthetase antibodies
Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Systemic sclerosis and overlap connective tissue disease
Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Myositis-specific and myositis-associated antibody panel including anti-Jo-1 and other anti-synthetase antibodies
Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes to assess myositis activity
High-resolution CT of the chest to characterise interstitial lung disease
Pulmonary function tests including gas transfer to quantify and monitor lung involvement
MRI of muscle and/or electromyography and muscle biopsy to confirm myositis
Nailfold capillaroscopy and autoimmune screen to define overlap features
redFlags: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with worsening dyspnoea and hypoxaemia
Severe or rapidly progressive muscle weakness including respiratory or bulbar muscles
Pulmonary hypertension complicating chronic lung disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the severity and progression of interstitial lung disease; many patients stabilise with immunosuppression, but rapidly progressive lung disease carries significant mortality, and relapses are common on treatment reduction.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in amyopathic patients who present with lung disease and normal creatine kinase
Failing to test the full anti-synthetase antibody panel when anti-Jo-1 is negative
Underestimating interstitial lung disease, the main determinant of outcome
Attributing mechanic's hands to occupational or eczematous skin change
Not screening for pulmonary hypertension in longstanding lung disease
management: Induce remission with systemic corticosteroids as first-line immunosuppression

Add a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate or a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or ciclosporin), the last being useful where interstitial lung disease dominates
Treat rapidly progressive or refractory interstitial lung disease aggressively with rituximab, cyclophosphamide or intravenous immunoglobulin
Monitor the prognosis-determining lung disease with serial high-resolution CT and pulmonary function tests including gas transfer, and track myositis activity with creatine kinase
Provide supportive care: physiotherapy for muscle weakness, emollients for mechanic's hands, and cold avoidance with a calcium-channel blocker for Raynaud phenomenon
Optimise respiratory support with pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and supplemental oxygen, and consider lung transplantation in end-stage fibrotic disease
Manage jointly through a rheumatology and respiratory multidisciplinary team, and screen for occult malignancy where clinically indicated
